title: Semantic search in four moves

kcs.statement: Embed documents offline, embed the query with the same model, rank by similarity, return the top-k.
Which steps run once and which run per query, and what each costs.

misconceptions.statement: Every query re-embeds the stored documents.
Asking for fewer results (a smaller k) means fewer documents get scored.
Editing or adding one document means re-embedding the whole collection.

glossary.md: Search by meaning: rank documents by the similarity of their embeddings to the query's embedding.
A passage cut from a document that is embedded and retrieved as a unit.
One run of the embedding model on one piece of text, giving that text's vector.
Work done once, before any query arrives: embed every document (or chunk) and store the vectors. Redone only for a document that is added or edited, or for all of them when the model changes.
Work done again for every query: embed the query with the same model, score it against every stored vector, sort, and keep the top-k.
The stored document vectors, each kept next to its document or chunk ID, that every query is scored against.
One multiplication whose result is added to a running total. A dot product of two vectors with d numbers takes d of them.

Scoring the query against every stored vector, then sorting. It always finds the true top-k, and costs N × d multiply-adds per query. Later units call it exact search and compare it with faster approximate indexes.

md: Now assemble the pieces into [[semantic search]]:
**Offline, once:** (1) split your documents into passages (*chunks*), (2) embed every chunk, and store the vectors next to their chunk IDs.
**Online, per query:** (3) embed the query with **the same model**, (4) score every stored vector against it (cosine), sort, and return the [[top-k]].

That's it. Everything in the Intermediate and Advanced layers is about doing these four moves *well*: what to embed, which model to use, how to score fast at scale, and how to measure whether it works.

block.goal_md: Step through indexing and querying. Watch a document turn into a vector and a query find its nearest neighbours.

tasks.prompt: Step through the whole pipeline to the final ranked results.
tasks.aha_md: Notice that the expensive part (embedding every document) happens once, offline. Per query you embed one short text and do a fast vector lookup.

block.title: Rank three help articles by hand
block.problem_md: Three help articles have 3-D toy embeddings: **D1** *Reset your password* `[0.9, 0.1, 0.0]`, **D2** *Track your parcel* `[0.0, 0.2, 0.95]`, **D3** *Update your billing card* `[0.1, 0.95, 0.1]`. The query *can't log in* embeds to `[0.8, 0.0, 0.1]`. Rank the articles.

steps.why_md: D2 and D3 are close. Small toy vectors make near-ties common, and real systems see them too.

block.answer_md: Ranking: **D1 (0.99)** ≫ D2 (0.12) > D3 (0.12). *Can't log in* shares no words with *Reset your password*, and it still finds it. That's semantic search.

options.why_md: Online step: happens per query, with the same model as the documents.

options.why_md: Offline step 1: decide the units you will retrieve.

options.md: Return the top-k chunks
options.why_md: The last step: sort by score and cut.

question.prompt_md: Your documents were embedded with model **A** last year. A new teammate embeds queries with model **B**, which has the same dimension count. What happens?

options.md: Results are effectively random
options.why_md: Right. Each model learns its own coordinate system. Same length doesn't mean same space: dimension 5 in A has nothing to do with dimension 5 in B.

options.md: It works, just slightly worse
options.why_md: It isn't “slightly worse”. Cross-model similarity scores have no meaning.

options.md: It works because both are 768-dimensional
options.why_md: Matching dimension counts only means the arithmetic runs. The meanings of the axes don't line up.

beats.title: Once vs every query: what search costs

md: The capstone runs 10 labelled queries against the 25-article help centre, and a live help centre answers queries all day. So before you code it, sort the four moves by **when** they run. Some work is done once and reused by every query. Some is done again for every single query.
Getting this split wrong is the classic first-prototype bug: the search runs the embedding model far more often than it needs to, and nothing in the results tells you.

question.prompt_md: All 25 help articles were embedded last night and their vectors are stored. A customer now types *where is my parcel?*. To answer this one query, how many times does the embedding model run?

options.md: 1: only the query is embedded
options.why_md: Right. The article vectors are already stored and don't depend on the query. Only the query's text still needs to become a vector.

options.md: 26: all 25 articles again, plus the query
options.why_md: That repeats last night's work. The articles haven't changed, so their stored vectors are still valid. Hold on to this guess: it is the bug this beat is about.

options.md: 25: once per article it is compared with
options.why_md: Comparing the query with an article is a dot product of their two vectors: arithmetic, not a model run. The model runs once for each text that still needs a vector.

options.md: 0: the query text is compared with the stored vectors directly
options.why_md: A text and a vector can't be compared. The query first has to become a vector, using the same model as the articles.

md: Split the four moves by when they run. One term first: a [[model call]] is one run of the embedding model on one piece of text, giving that text's vector.

The [[offline step]] happens before any query exists: one model call per article, and each vector is stored next to its article ID. That stored collection is the [[index]]. Nothing in it depends on a query, so every query reuses it. You only touch it again when an article is added or edited (embed just that article) or when you switch models (embed every article again, because a new model means a new space).
The [[online step]] happens for every query: (1) one model call to embed the query, with the same model; (2) a score for every stored vector; (3) sort the scores and keep the [[top-k]].

Step (2) has a cost you can count. A dot product of two vectors with $d$ numbers multiplies position 1 by position 1, position 2 by position 2, and so on, adding each product to a running total. Each multiply-then-add is one [[multiply-add]], so one dot product costs $d$ multiply-adds. Scoring the query against all $N$ stored vectors is called [[brute-force search]]. It costs $N \times d$ multiply-adds for every query, whatever k is.

Picture a library card catalogue. A card is written once, when a book arrives: that's offline. Each visitor's question is new: that's online. With brute force, someone checks the question against every card, for every visitor.

block.tex: \text{offline, once: } N \text{ model calls} \qquad \text{online, per query: } 1 \text{ model call},\;\; N \times d \text{ multiply-adds},\;\; \text{a sort of } N \text{ scores}
block.explain_md: Keep the kinds of work in separate columns instead of adding them up: one model call runs a whole neural network over a text, which is far more arithmetic than one multiply-add. What matters here is **which work repeats**. Only the right-hand side is paid again for every query.

parts.means: number of stored vectors (one per article here; one per chunk once articles are split)
numbers per vector, the model's dimension count (384 for all-MiniLM-L6-v2)
one multiply-add for every stored number, per query

block.title: Count the work for the help centre by hand
block.problem_md: The help centre has **25** articles. The model outputs **384** numbers per text (like `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` from the last topic), and stored vectors are scored with a dot product. Count the model calls and multiply-adds (a) to build the index, (b) for a first query *can't log in*, (c) for a second query *where is my parcel?*, and (d) for all 10 labelled queries.

steps.md: **(a) Offline.** One model call per article: **25 model calls**. The index stores $25 \times 384 = 9{,}600$ numbers, each vector next to its article ID.
steps.why_md: This happens once. It is the only time the articles go through the model.

steps.md: **(b) Query 1, embed.** One model call turns *can't log in* into a 384-number query vector, with the same model as the articles.
**(b) Query 1, score.** One dot product per stored vector: $25 \times 384 = 9{,}600$ multiply-adds. Then sort the 25 scores and keep the top 3.
steps.why_md: 9,600 again, and not by coincidence: each of the 9,600 stored numbers is multiplied by its matching query number exactly once.

steps.md: **(c) Query 2.** The 25 stored vectors are reused as they are: **0** article embeddings. The cost is the same as query 1: 1 model call, 9,600 multiply-adds and a sort of 25 scores.
steps.why_md: The index doesn't depend on which query comes next. Only the query vector is new.

steps.md: **(d) All 10 labelled queries.** Model calls: $25 + 10 \times 1 = 35$. Multiply-adds: $10 \times 9{,}600 = 96{,}000$.

block.answer_md: Offline: **25 model calls**, once. Per query: **1 model call**, **9,600 multiply-adds** and a sort of 25 scores. Code that re-embedded the articles for every query would make $10 \times (25 + 1) = 260$ model calls for the 10 queries instead of 35.

tasks.prompt: Run the bench's labelled queries: set the number of queries to 10.
tasks.aha_md: Each extra query adds 1 model call; the re-embedding version adds N + 1. With 25 articles and 10 queries that is 35 calls against 260. Offline work is paid once, however many queries follow.

tasks.prompt: Double the help centre to 50 articles.
tasks.aha_md: Multiply-adds per query double: 50 × 384 = 19,200. Embedding offline doesn't make queries free. Every stored vector is still scored, so online cost grows with N.

tasks.prompt: Switch to a model with 768 numbers per vector.
tasks.aha_md: Every dot product is twice as long, so per-query scoring doubles. A new model is also a new space: every article must be re-embedded offline before the first query.

block.title: “Every search re-embeds the documents”
md: The article vectors don't depend on the query, so they are computed once, offline, and stored. A query embeds **only itself**.

Re-embed an article when its text changes (just that one), and re-embed all of them only when you switch models. If your search function calls the model on every article each time it runs, that's this bug: correct results, and a cost that grows with every query.

question.prompt_md: The help centre grows to **200** articles. Same 384-number model, dot-product scoring, and the page shows the **top 3**. How many multiply-adds does brute-force scoring take for **one** query?

common_wrong.why_md: $3 \times 384$ scores only the three results. You can't know which three are best until all 200 articles are scored; k only decides where the sorted list is cut.
That counts dot products. Each dot product is 384 multiply-adds.

question.hint_md: One dot product per stored vector, and $d$ multiply-adds per dot product.
question.solution_md: $200 \times 384 = 76{,}800$ multiply-adds. The top-3 cut happens after scoring and doesn't change this.

question.prompt_md: The article *Update your billing card* is rewritten. The model stays the same. What must happen so search reflects the new text?

options.md: Re-embed that one article and replace its stored vector
options.why_md: Right. A vector depends on two things, the text and the model. Only this article's text changed, so only its vector is stale.

options.md: Re-embed all 25 articles
options.why_md: The other 24 texts and the model are unchanged, so their vectors are still right. Re-embedding everything is only needed when you switch models.

options.md: Nothing: the next query re-embeds it anyway
options.why_md: Queries embed only themselves. Without a re-embed, the index keeps scoring the old text.

options.md: Nothing: the title didn't change, so the vector still matches
options.why_md: The vector came from the article's text, not just its title. Changed text means a stale vector.

question.solution_md: Embed the rewritten article once and replace its vector in the index. Everything else stays.

recap.formula: offline, once: N model calls · online, per query: 1 model call + N × d multiply-adds + a sort of N scores
recap.template: chunk → embed (offline) · embed query → rank → top-k (per query)
recap.pitfall: Embedding the query with a different model than the documents silently breaks ranking.

anticipated_doubts.question: Why must the query use the same model as the documents?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: Every model invents its own coordinate system while training. In model A, dimension 5 might partly track “finance-ness”; in model B, dimension 5 tracks something unrelated. Comparing a vector from A with one from B is like comparing GPS coordinates with street addresses. Both are locations, in incompatible systems.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: Two cartographers each draw a map of the same city, with different scales, orientations and origins. A point at (3, 4) on map A and (3, 4) on map B are different places. Embeddings from different models are maps by different cartographers.

bridge.title: Two maps, one city
md: Each embedding model is a **map of meaning**. Train two models and you get two maps of the same city, rotated, stretched and shifted differently.

- Points on the **same** map: distances mean something.
- A point from map A against a point on map B: the number is meaningless, even when both maps use 1,536 coordinates.
So: **one index, one model, one version**. Store the `model_id` with every vector.

verify.prompt_md: You re-train your embedding model on new data (same architecture, same 768 dims). Existing index vectors:

options.md: Must be re-embedded: retraining produces a new space
options.why_md: Right. Even the same architecture lands in a different coordinate system after retraining.

options.md: Are still valid, since the architecture is unchanged
options.why_md: Weights changed, so the map changed.

options.md: Need only re-normalization
options.why_md: Normalizing doesn't align two spaces.

anticipated_doubts.question: How do I choose k?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: k is simply how many results you hand back, so choose it from what happens next: a help page might show 3 to 5 article links, and nobody reads 50. Changing k doesn't change any score. Every article is scored and sorted the same way; k only decides where you cut the list. Whether the right article actually lands inside the top k is something you measure later, in *Measuring retrieval*.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: Think of a results page with room for three links. You still rank every article, then show the first three. If the page grows to five slots, the ranking is identical; you just show two more rows of it.

bridge.title: Same scores, different k
md: Scores for five articles, already sorted: password 0.91, login 0.82, billing 0.67, refund 0.31, parcel 0.12.

- k = 3 → password, login, billing.
- k = 5 → the same three, then refund and parcel.
Raising k never reorders the top of the list. It only shows more of it.

verify.prompt_md: You raise k from 3 to 5 for the same query. What happens to the first three results?

options.md: They stay the same; two more results appear after them
options.why_md: Right. k only decides where the sorted list is cut.

options.md: They can change, because more articles get compared
options.why_md: Every article was already scored for k = 3. The scores and their order don't depend on k.

options.md: Their scores drop, because the score is shared among more results
options.why_md: Each score is a cosine (or dot product) of the query with one article on its own. It isn't a share of a total.

anticipated_doubts.question: When do the articles need to be embedded again?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: In two cases only. (1) An article is added or its text changes: embed **that article** and add or replace its vector. The other vectors came from unchanged text and the same model, so they are still right. (2) You switch to a different model, or a new version of it: embed **every** article again, because the new model's vectors live in a different space (*What an embedding model is*). A new query never re-embeds articles.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: An article's vector depends on exactly two things: its text and the model. Ask whether either changed. Text changed: redo that article. Model changed: redo every article. Neither: reuse the stored vector.

bridge.title: What changed decides what to redo
md:
| What changed | Articles to re-embed |
|---|---|
| One article's text | That one article |
| A new article arrives | That one article |
| The model | Every article |
| Nothing: a new query arrives | None; embed only the query |

verify.prompt_md: This week 3 of the 25 articles were edited, 1 new article was added, and the model stayed the same. How many article embeddings must the system run?

options.why_md: Right: the 3 edited articles plus the new one. The other 22 vectors are unchanged.
That re-embeds all 26 articles. Only a model change requires that.

options.md: 0: the next query will embed them
options.why_md: Queries embed only themselves. Articles are embedded offline.

anticipated_doubts.question: Cosine also divides by the vector lengths. Doesn't that add to the per-query cost?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: A little, and most of it can move offline. Cosine is $\dfrac{q \cdot v}{\|q\|\,\|v\|}$. Each article's length $\|v\|$ depends only on the article, so compute it once offline and store it next to the vector. The query's length $\|q\|$ costs $d$ more multiply-adds **once per query**, not once per article. Per query that adds $N$ divisions to the $N \times d$ multiply-adds. And because $\|q\|$ is the same number in all $N$ scores, dividing by it can't change the ranking.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: Divide every score by the same positive number, say 2: 0.8 becomes 0.4 and 0.6 becomes 0.3. Smaller, but in the same order. The query's length is that same number for every article.

bridge.title: Where the length work goes
md: For 25 articles at 384 numbers each:

- Offline, once: 25 article lengths, 384 multiply-adds each.
- Per query: the query's length (384 multiply-adds), 25 dot products (9,600 multiply-adds) and 25 divisions.
The dot products are still most of the per-query arithmetic. *Metrics and normalisation* later shows how scaling every vector to length 1 offline removes the divisions altogether.

verify.prompt_md: Every article's score is divided by the same positive number (the query's length). What happens to the ranking?

options.md: Nothing: dividing every score by the same positive number keeps their order
options.why_md: Right. Each score shrinks by the same factor, so no article overtakes another.

options.md: Articles with longer vectors move up
options.why_md: Every score is divided by the same number, so no article gains on another.

options.md: The order reverses
options.why_md: Dividing by a positive number keeps the order. Only a negative number would flip it.

anticipated_doubts.question: If I only want the top 3, why score all 25 articles?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: Because scores don't arrive in order. Until an article is scored you don't know where it ranks, so stopping after three decent matches can miss a better one further down the list. Brute-force search scores all $N$ stored vectors and then cuts: $N \times d$ multiply-adds per query, whatever k is. Indexes that skip most vectors, and accept occasionally missing a true top result, are the subject of *Retrieval at scale*; they pay off only when N gets large.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: To name the three tallest people in a room you have to look at everyone. Stopping after the first three tall people you notice can miss the tallest one standing at the back.

bridge.title: The three tallest in the room
md: To name the three tallest of 25 people, you measure all 25, then pick the top three.
Measuring only until you've seen three tall people is quicker, but the tallest might be the 24th person you'd have measured.
Brute-force search is measure-everyone: it always finds the true top-k, and it pays $N \times d$ multiply-adds per query to do it.

verify.prompt_md: 40 articles, 384 numbers per vector, brute-force scoring with dot products, and k = 1. How many multiply-adds does scoring take per query?

common_wrong.why_md: That scores only one article. All 40 must be scored to know which one is best.
